title: Industrial-cost proof-carrying software

concept.text: The innovation would make rigorous software assurance practical at ordinary development costs: a team would specify what a large production system must do, implement it in a usable programming language, and deliver executable machine code together with machine-checkable evidence that it satisfies stated functional-correctness, memory-safety, and information-flow properties. The intended advance includes affordable development and maintenance, so that changing the software and repairing its proofs becomes a routine engineering activity.

Three distinct achievements must connect. Application verification establishes that a program meets its specification. Compiler verification establishes that compilation preserves the relevant program behavior. Proof-carrying delivery supplies evidence about the delivered artifact that a trusted checker can independently validate. A verified compiler does not automatically prove an application's requirements, and a proof about source code does not automatically cover the final binary. The proposed capability would connect these layers while making their remaining assumptions explicit.

significance.text: Machine-checked proofs can exclude entire specified classes of unwanted behavior under explicit models and assumptions. If this assurance became affordable for large systems, developers could routinely ship artifacts with checked evidence for their stated safety and security properties before execution. Operating systems, compilers, cryptographic stacks, and controllers are plausible beneficiaries. Hoare's 2003 verifying-compiler challenge provides the underlying vision; extending it across these domains at ordinary costs remains a conditional impact judgment.

seL4 supplies a concrete basis for taking this prospect seriously. Its project reports no functional-correctness defects in verified code since the first functional-correctness proof completed in 2009, across more than fifteen years of testing, use, and deployment. This is a reported observation about the verified code within its proof scope and assumptions. It does not independently certify every configuration, surrounding component, or aspect of system behavior.

The impact depends on choosing adequate specifications and models. A program can faithfully implement an inadequate specification; a software proof also depends on assumptions about its execution environment. Functional correctness alone does not establish that a controller meets deadlines or that a physical system remains safe. Timing, device behavior, and relevant environmental constraints need their own specifications and supporting guarantees. These boundaries matter when projecting benefits into medicine, vehicles, or infrastructure.

Scientific scope clarification: the proposal would not provide a general decision procedure for termination or all nontrivial semantic properties of unrestricted programs. Its practical route is to work with explicit specifications, suitable languages and abstractions, and proof obligations that may require human guidance or remain unproved. One successful large-system demonstration would establish feasibility within its scope; routine use across many domains would require broader evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is an integrated specification-to-executable process whose total effort is comparable to ordinary implementation and testing. The supplied evidence establishes substantial component achievements and motivates this target, but it does not establish that the complete capability is absent everywhere as of November 1, 2026. The open engineering question supported by this record is how to combine strong specifications, scalable verification, trustworthy compilation, independently checkable evidence, and affordable maintenance in realistic production development.

The historical seL4 effort illustrates why cost is central. At its first proof completion in 2009, approximately 7,500 of 8,700 lines of C were verified using about 200,000 lines of Isabelle proof script. Design, documentation, implementation, and verification together required about 25 person-years, including research, tool development, and libraries. That total is not a measurement of proof labor alone, nor a controlled estimate of the overhead relative to ordinary development. Assembly and kernel boot code were outside that verified coverage.

Concrete scope barriers include concurrency, kernel initialization, hardware abstractions, and the connection between software behavior and execution time. The July 2026 seL4 slides report multicore verification in progress, unverified initialization code, and abstract models of the MMU and caches. Abstract cache modeling is different from having no cache model, but it limits which hardware-level conclusions follow. CompCert addresses another layer by proving semantic preservation for compilation of a large C subset to assembly; that result does not itself prove an operating system's application-level specification or every subsequent step to a deployed binary.

Engineering synthesis: an affordable integrated process would need reusable specifications and proof components, automation that handles common obligations, manageable interfaces between components, and proof repair that keeps pace with software changes. It would also need to expose unsupported features and unproved obligations clearly. Lowering the cost by weakening the specification would not establish the intended combination of functional correctness, memory safety, and information-flow assurance.

current_state.text: The supplied seL4 materials document an achieved verified microkernel component. Its kernel implementation is approximately 10,000 lines of C, depending on configuration. Functional-correctness proofs establish that the C code of verified configurations behaves according to the seL4 specification; binary-correctness and security guarantees depend on the configuration and available proofs. These are substantial results, but they do not establish verification of an entire commodity operating system, browser, or million-line application.

The 2009 proof statistics provide a dated baseline: 8,700 C lines, 7,500 verified C lines, roughly 200,000 Isabelle proof-script lines, and about 25 person-years for the combined design-through-verification effort. A 2015 note reports that related proof files had grown to approximately 500,000 lines. Those later files have a different scope from the original proof-script count, so the two figures should not be treated as directly comparable measures of productivity or proof complexity.

The July 2026 OSPERT slides list initialization code as unverified, describe MMU and cache models as abstract, and state that multicore verification is in progress. Separately, the seL4 proofs page describes verified user-level system initialization in supported configurations: an initializer configures a system to conform to a supplied description. This does not establish verification of kernel boot code. Distinguishing these components reconciles the apparent tension between the initialization statements.

The supplied CompCert documentation identifies version 3.18, dated August 31, 2026. It describes compilation from CompCert C, a large subset of C, to ARM, PowerPC, RISC-V, and x86 assembly, with a semantic-preservation guarantee. This is a compiler achievement with a defined language and target scope. It is distinct from proving application requirements, supporting every C feature, or establishing a complete proof through assembly and linking to a deployed executable. The retained documentation is an introduction and index, rather than the complete proof development.

Hoare's January 2003 paper articulates the verifying-compiler goal, including large-scale use and independently checked proofs. The supplied source collection does not establish how widely such methods are adopted in industry, which verified systems are largest or strongest across the field, or whether the complete cost target had been achieved by November 2026. The July and August 2026 materials support statements at their documented dates; the supplied review contains no broader freshness search establishing an exhaustive November picture.

The original 2009 SOSP page was not captured in the supplied evidence. Its precise original compiler and hardware assumption wording therefore cannot be confirmed from that artifact here. The retained seL4 proofs page supports the broader need to state trusted assumptions. The linked seL4 manual also has truncated text and extraction gaps, so it is not used here to infer additional configuration coverage. These access limitations leave details unresolved; they do not show that the underlying results are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scale demonstration: build a production-scale system containing at least one million implementation lines, concurrency, and a real device interface. Compile it through a verified toolchain to a deployed binary and provide machine-checked evidence for a published specification explicitly covering functional correctness, memory safety, and information flow. Publish a reproducible line-count method and identify generated code, libraries, excluded components, and verified configurations. The million-line threshold is a proposed scale proxy, not an established community standard.
completion_criteria.label: Million-line production system with machine-checked guarantees reaching deployed binary

completion_criteria.text: Proposed assurance demonstration: publish the source, specifications, proof artifacts, toolchain versions, checker, and reproducible build instructions. Independent teams should be able to rebuild the executable and check the evidence. Document the trusted computing base, concurrency semantics, device and hardware models, initialization coverage, and every unverified transformation between source and deployed code. State precisely which claims reach the binary and which depend on external assumptions. If timing or physical safety is claimed, require corresponding models and proofs.
completion_criteria.label: Independent rebuilds and proof checks with documented trust assumptions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed cost demonstration: define an ordinary unverified development baseline and the permitted small multiple of its effort before evaluating success. Count specification work, implementation, testing, proof construction, tool adaptation, integration, and proof repair. Include maintenance over a stated interval with representative feature changes and defect fixes. Report performance, resource use, and supported language features so that low verification cost cannot conceal impractical runtime behavior or an artificially restricted workload.
completion_criteria.label: Development and maintenance effort within predefined small baseline multiple

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth demonstration: repeat the process with independent teams and materially different systems, such as a systems component, cryptographic stack, and controller, while reporting where automation fails and how much expert intervention is required. A first successful system would demonstrate feasibility; repeated affordable development and maintenance would support a claim of industrial routine. Finite demonstrations establish the breadth actually tested, never literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams repeat affordable verification across materially different systems

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — CSC-10, Machine-checked behavioral guarantees for frontier learned models, has the closest assurance overlap. Both can use specifications, proof infrastructure, and verified toolchains. CSC-04 concerns the correctness of software against explicit requirements; it does not by itself establish the behavioral adequacy of a learned model. The roster supplies no fuller CSC-10 definition, so the exact boundary remains provisional.

Roster-based synthesis — CSC-07, Reliable machine-checked mathematical discovery, could contribute proof search, reusable mathematics, or proof-assistant infrastructure. Its central object is mathematical discovery, whereas CSC-04 includes executable software, compilation, deployment assumptions, and lifecycle cost. CSC-01, Practical polynomial-time algorithms for NP-complete problems, could potentially affect some verification subproblems, but CSC-04 neither requires nor establishes that algorithmic breakthrough. Faster search would not automatically supply adequate specifications.

Roster-based synthesis — CSC-05, Routine-cost general computation on encrypted data, and CSC-09, Practical indistinguishability obfuscation, address different forms of confidentiality. CSC-04 could help establish that implementations of those techniques meet specified requirements, including relevant information-flow properties. Verifying an implementation would not itself create efficient encrypted computation or establish the cryptographic assumptions behind obfuscation.

Roster-based synthesis — CSC-03, Competent general machine intelligence, could potentially assist specification, implementation, and proof construction; CSC-04's criterion would still be independently checkable evidence and measured engineering cost. CSC-06, A predictive theory of generalization for modern learning systems, concerns learned behavior beyond training experience. Such a theory could inform model specifications, but ordinary software correctness does not supply it.

Roster-based synthesis — CSC-08, General-purpose physical autonomy in unmodified environments, could benefit from verified controllers and supporting software, while still requiring adequate perception, environment models, timing guarantees, and physical validation. CSC-02, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computation, could use verification methods for supporting software and toolchains, but proving classical software properties does not establish fault-tolerant quantum hardware or application-scale quantum performance.

unresolved_issues: Whether any system had achieved the complete integrated capability and cost target by November 1, 2026 is not established by the supplied evidence.
The precise original compiler and hardware assumptions in the uncaptured 2009 SOSP artifact remain unconfirmed here.
The July 2026 limitations do not establish subsequent multicore or kernel-initialization progress, and the supplied materials do not enumerate every verified configuration.
The ordinary-development baseline, permitted effort multiple, maintenance interval, and line-count conventions remain choices to define before evaluating the proposed demonstration.
The exact boundary with CSC-10 remains provisional because only its title, rather than a detailed concept definition, was supplied.

brief.title: Software with affordable proof that it works
possible: You could use large software systems that arrive with mathematical evidence that they meet stated requirements, use memory safely and keep information from flowing where it is forbidden. A computer could independently check that evidence for the executable you actually run.
Development teams could build and update this software at costs comparable to ordinary development and testing. Repairing proofs after a change would become routine engineering work.
why: Checked proofs could rule out whole classes of software errors before a program runs. Affordable proofs would bring that assurance into routine development of operating systems, tools that translate programs, software that protects encrypted data, and controllers.

sources.showed: Hoare proposed a tool that uses mathematical reasoning to check programs against stated requirements, with independently checked proofs and use across large bodies of software.
sources.cited_for: The goal is to make checked software correctness part of everyday development and maintenance.
sources.not_established: The proposal does not demonstrate an affordable process that delivers large executable systems with checked proofs.

sources.showed: The project proved that supported versions of seL4, a small operating-system core, meet their specification. Some versions also have proofs covering executable code and security.
sources.quote:
there have been no functional correctness defects in
  verified code since the functional correctness proof completed in 2009
sources.cited_for: Strong proofs can cover running code and exclude specified classes of errors.
sources.not_established: The guarantees depend on the configuration and assumptions; they do not cover an entire operating system or establish ordinary development costs.

sources.showed: The original seL4 effort required about 25 person-years, including design, documentation, implementation, verification and research tools.
sources.quote:
In total, design, documentation, implementation and verification
of the seL4 kernel come to about 25 person years.
sources.cited_for: Affordability must include the full development effort, rather than proof checking alone.
sources.not_established: The historical total does not isolate proof overhead or compare it with a matched ordinary development project.

sources.who: Simon Sillitoe, Abdul Basit, Massimiliano Giacometti and Gernot Heiser
sources.showed: The team restored an analysis that estimates seL4's longest execution time. It completed the full analysis, but placeholder hardware timings leave the result an estimate.
sources.quote: All full-kernel cache analyses: from infeasible to ≈ 1 h
sources.cited_for: Meeting a behavior specification and meeting a deadline require separate guarantees.
sources.not_established: The restored analysis does not yet provide a timing guarantee based on sound hardware timings and verified execution bounds.

sources.showed: CompCert is a compiler, a tool that translates programs. Its checked proof establishes that translation from a large subset of C to assembly, a written form of processor instructions, preserves program behavior.
sources.quote:
the fact that the generated assembly code is
semantically equivalent to its source program --- was entirely proved
within the Coq proof assistant.
sources.cited_for: Translation can preserve proved program behavior through to assembly.
sources.not_established: This does not prove application requirements or cover every subsequent step from assembly to the deployed executable.

shown: The seL4 project has proved that an operating-system core of roughly 10,000 lines behaves as specified in supported configurations. Some configurations connect those guarantees to executable code and include security proofs.

CompCert proves that translating supported C programs preserves their behavior through to assembly. Together, these results demonstrate important parts of the path from requirements to running software.
missing: A large production demonstration needs to connect requirements, program proofs, translation and independently checkable evidence for deployed code.
Development and maintenance need to meet a predefined cost target without weakening requirements or making the software impractical.
Independent teams need to repeat affordable verification across substantially different kinds of systems.

milestones.label: A million-line system with proofs covering deployed code
milestones.explanation: A million-line system with tasks running together and a real device interface would need proofs covering specified behavior, safe memory use and permitted information flows through deployed code. This would test production scale.

milestones.label: Independent teams rebuild the software and check its proofs
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to rebuild the executable and check its proofs, with all trusted tools, hardware assumptions and coverage limits explicit. This would establish which guarantees others can reproduce.

milestones.label: Development and upkeep meet a predefined cost target
milestones.explanation: Total development and maintenance effort would have to stay within a predefined small multiple of ordinary development, with practical performance and language support. This would establish affordability through representative changes.

milestones.label: Independent teams repeat affordable verification across different systems
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat affordable development and maintenance across materially different systems, reporting expert effort and automation failures. This would support routine industrial use across the tested domains.

uncertain: A proof can establish that software follows its requirements while those requirements still omit behavior that users need.
Timing and physical safety need their own models and proofs; correct software behavior alone does not establish them.
The ordinary-development baseline, allowed cost multiple, maintenance interval and rules for counting code remain to be defined.

page.title: Proof-carrying code at development and maintenance cost parity
page.definition: Production machine code would carry independently checkable proofs of its stated behaviour, memory safety (valid memory accesses) and information flow (permitted transfers between security domains). Total development and maintenance cost, including proofs, would not exceed that of equivalent software developed and tested without proofs.

goal.need: Of 912 high- or critical-severity bugs examined in stable Chrome releases, about 70% involved memory safety. Tests give little evidence about inputs they never exercise. An operator updating a network service could check, before running it, that every execution covered by the proof respects its memory and information-flow rules. At cost parity, suppliers could maintain that assurance within their ordinary development and maintenance budgets. Its value depends on the rules capturing users’ needs and on the execution assumptions holding.

statements.quote: A verifying compiler uses mathematical and logical reasoning to check the correctness of the programs that it compiles.

statements.quote: HACMS seeks a synthesizer capable of producing a machine-checkable proof that the generated code satisfies functional specifications as well as security and safety policies.

statements.context: The goal concerns verified replacements for software already in service and the preservation of verification through later changes.

completion.title: Production code carries executable-level proofs at development and maintenance cost parity.
completion.criterion: For a production software system, independently check proofs that its delivered executable meets a published functional specification, memory-safety rules and information-flow policy, under explicit execution assumptions. Demonstrate total development and maintenance cost ≤1.0 times a matched implementation-and-testing baseline with the same functionality, performance requirements and change workload. Include labour for specification, integration, testing, proof construction and repair, plus tools and computation. Fix the baseline, costing method, workload and maintenance interval before comparison.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational definition; no joint external acceptance test located.
completion.basis: Searched Hoare’s challenge, DARPA HACMS and PROVERS rules, and formal-verification standards, cost benchmarks and industrial acceptance thresholds. No published test combining executable-level proofs with whole-lifecycle cost parity was found. The 1.0 cost ratio operationalises ordinary development cost; it is an Atlas choice. PROVERS’s proof-edit percentage does not measure total cost.

milestones.title: A code consumer validates a supplied binary’s safety proof before executing the binary.
milestones.criterion: Before executing a supplied native-code binary, the consumer checks its accompanying proof against the binary and the consumer’s published safety policy. Validation must establish that the code obeys the policy whenever the stated entry conditions hold.
milestones.set_by: Proof-carrying-code research convention; Necula and Lee’s OSDI 1996 protocol, instantiated for packet filters.
milestones.threshold_quote: Kernel safety is ensured by validating the safety proof.

milestones.title: A software implementation has a machine-checked proof that it refines its functional specification.
milestones.criterion: A proof assistant checks that every observable behaviour of the implementation under the stated execution assumptions is permitted by its abstract functional specification. Identify the implementation level to which the theorem applies.
milestones.set_by: Functional-verification community’s refinement criterion, instantiated by the seL4 team in SOSP 2009.
milestones.threshold_quote: Functional correctness means here that the implementation always strictly follows our high-level abstract specification of kernel behaviour.

milestones.title: A compiler has a machine-checked semantic-preservation proof from its source language to assembly.
milestones.criterion: Machine-check a theorem covering every successful compilation in the supported source language. When the source program has defined behaviour, every observable behaviour of the generated assembly must be permitted by the source semantics.
milestones.set_by: Compiler-verification community’s semantic-preservation criterion, formalised in CompCert’s documentation and Compiler module.
milestones.threshold_quote: the fact that the generated assembly code is semantically equivalent to its source program

milestones.title: A system’s executable inherits functional-correctness and information-flow guarantees from its source.
milestones.criterion: Prove that the executable refines the source semantics used in the functional-correctness proof. For that same executable and configuration, establish that the functional specification and the information-flow policy both hold. State the execution assumptions and the observations covered by the information-flow theorem.
milestones.set_by: Binary-refinement and information-flow verification conventions; Sewell, Myreen and Klein’s PLDI 2013 result and the seL4 proof statements.
milestones.threshold_quote: Formally, we prove that the binary is a refinement of the stated C source semantics.

milestones.title: Developers prove >10 property classes, with <5% of serious findings left and 1% of proof lines edited by hand.
milestones.criterion: Apply the tentative PROVERS Phase 3 targets to a high-complexity system. Developers without formal-methods expertise demonstrate the tools. More than 10 classes of system properties are proved, and less than 5% of serious findings by the red team remain. After software updates and maintenance, measure the percentage of proof lines requiring manual change against the 1% target.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, PROVERS broad agency announcement HR001123S0020, Table 1, Phase 3 Maturation column, and programme FAQ on developer participation.
milestones.threshold_quote:
lines of proof requiring manual change following software update and maintenance

20% 10% 1%

milestones.title: A production project rechecks its proofs on every code change submitted for integration.
milestones.criterion: Integrate proof checking into the project’s build workflow so that each pushed change or pull request triggers a check of the stated properties against the updated implementation. A successful run must establish those properties for the revision under test.
milestones.set_by: Continuous formal verification practice in the Amazon s2n deployment, identified in DARPA’s PROVERS FAQ as the precedent for proof maintenance.
milestones.threshold_quote:
runs every time a code change is
pushed or a pull request is issued.

milestones.title: Evaluators compare proof-tool costs and development efficiency against a baseline workflow.
milestones.criterion: Document the platform team’s baseline workflow. Compare the continuous proof workflow with traditional formal verification, evaluating the costs of scaling, using, adopting and maintaining the tools and their effect on development efficiency. Report the comparison without imposing a numerical cost ratio.
milestones.set_by: DARPA, PROVERS broad agency announcement HR001123S0020, quantitative evaluation and evidence curation requirements.
milestones.threshold_quote: cost (of scaling, use, adoption, and maintenance).

results.detail: The theorem covers the modeled x86 instruction subset and assumes strong sequential consistency for atomic instructions. The model omits the TLB, and the assembler, bootloader, PreInit module and ELF loader are unverified.
results.quote:
We
have successfully developed a practical concurrent OS
kernel and veriﬁed its (contextual) functional correctness
in Coq.

results.finding: Functional correctness reaches modeled x86 assembly for one concurrent kernel, mC2.
results.detail: The prior information-flow result appears in related work. The mC2 model omits TLB behavior and leaves the bootloader, PreInit module and ELF loader unverified.

All global
properties proved at the system-call speciﬁcation level

results.detail: The checks cover null dereferences, unintended side effects, signed computations and reference equality. The text gives no fuzzing sample size.

results.detail: The functional assurance for generated Java depends on correct compilation and accurate models of the Java libraries.
results.quote:
The final iteration of AuthV2java
agreed with AuthV1 on 1015 inputs with no observed differ-
ences.

results.finding: One production project, AuthV2, reduced wall-clock proof checking to under 10 minutes.
results.detail: A brittleness report measures solver stability. The milestone also requires a successful run to establish the functional properties for the submitted revision.
results.quote:
we could keep the wall-clock
verification time from 30 to below 10 minutes

results.finding: One AuthV2 replacement project took four years to develop.
results.detail: The discussion of other verification approaches does not provide comparative cost or development-efficiency measurements.
results.quote:
Over a period of four years we developed a new, for-
mally verified authorization engine, called AuthV2, that is
behaviorally equivalent to the original engine, called AuthV1.2

results.finding: One CakeML compiler source implementation has a HOL4 proof of its specified I/O behavior.
results.detail: The theorem assumes well-formed command-line arguments and a standard initial file-system state. The functional specification describes printing the compiler interface's return values.
results.quote:
Thus, we now have a CakeML program that is veriﬁed
to have the desired I/O behaviour of the CakeML compiler.

results.finding: One CakeML compiler has a HOL4 preservation theorem for five architectures that permits early resource-limit termination.
results.detail: The theorem assumes compatible compiler and machine configurations, correct installation, matching FFI behavior and environmental interference outside the CakeML process state.
results.quote:
behave the same as the source up to some point at which it terminates with an
out-of-memory error.

results.finding: One bootstrapped CakeML compiler has a HOL4 functional-correctness theorem for its machine code.
results.detail: Native execution assumes correct installation, matching FFI behavior and restricted environmental interference. The wrapper assembly used to establish the initial state is unverified.
results.quote:
This bootstrapping method produces a
machine code implementation of the compiler and also proves a theorem stating functional
correctness of that machine code.

results.finding: The s2n TLS handshake refinement proof covers 2 LLVM-level state-machine functions.
results.detail: The HMAC checks also establish functional agreement within their checked scope. They assume correct hash implementations, and the link to the monolithic specification uses sampled key and message sizes.
results.quote:
Formally, we proved that the implementation reﬁnes
a speciﬁcation (conversely, the speciﬁcation simulates the implementation).

results.finding: Amazon s2n recorded 956 CI proof replays on the upstream repository.
results.detail: Some replays were triggered by changes outside the verified code. The HMAC specification-level Coq proofs are rerun when the monolithic specification changes.
results.quote:
Since deployment of the proof to the CI system in November of 2016 our
proofs have been re-played 956 times.

results.finding: Across 3 s2n verification efforts, the TLS handshake took 8 months of engineering effort.
results.detail: Reported effort includes understanding the C code, specifying behavior, proving code against specifications, integrating CI and merging artifacts. The handshake effort also includes tool extensions for protocol reasoning.
results.quote:
The
TLS handshake veriﬁcation took longer at 8 months, though some of that time
involved developing tool extensions to support reasoning about protocols.

results.finding: Special J demonstrates host-side safety proof checking for native x86 code, with one worked method covering a four-byte array read.
results.detail: The worked proof covers the optimized loop in Poly.eval. The prototype checks type and memory safety under its entry and trusted-runtime assumptions. The supplied text identifies the publication as PLDI 2000 conference proceedings.

results.finding: The s2n TLS handshake refinement proof covers 2 functions that drive the state machine, analyzed as LLVM IR.
results.detail: The high-level specification models the subset of TLS 1.2 implemented by s2n. The verdict rests on the handshake refinement result. The HMAC checks separately sampled message sizes.
results.quote:
Formally, we proved that the implementation reﬁnes
a speciﬁcation (conversely, the speciﬁcation simulates the implementation).

results.finding: Amazon s2n recorded 956 proof replays in its main repository after integrating proof checks into CI.
results.detail: The replay count excludes forks and includes runs where the checked code was unchanged. The separate Coq proofs tied to the monolithic HMAC specification were rerun when that specification changed.
results.quote:
Since deployment of the proof to the CI system in November of 2016 our
proofs have been re-played 956 times.

results.finding: Across 3 s2n component verification projects, the TLS handshake took 8 months of engineering effort.
results.detail: The reported effort includes understanding the C code, writing specifications and proofs, integrating CI, and merging the proof artifacts. The handshake estimate also includes some tool development.
results.quote:
The
TLS handshake veriﬁcation took longer at 8 months, though some of that time
involved developing tool extensions to support reasoning about protocols.

results.finding: Lean checked a conditional fault-freedom proof against the bytes of one AArch64 libsignal-cli executable.
results.detail: The gatekeeper accepts proofs after Lean kernel replay and comparison with the approved specification. The paper gives no execution gate controlled by a code consumer.
results.quote: The theorem also establishes progress: every reachable valid call exits or aborts, and never faults or diverges.

results.finding: For one AArch64 libsignal-cli executable, Lean proved functional refinement for all runs of three covered operations under stated assumptions.
results.detail: Assumptions include bounded inputs, a fresh single-threaded process with only standard streams open, an empty environment, a fixed clock, randomness from a file, 1 GiB of memory beyond loaded segments, an 8 MiB stack and conforming hooks.
results.quote:
These theorems state that the executable implements the Lean models of
libsignal
on which the security proofs are built.

results.finding: One AArch64 libsignal-cli build satisfies ten symbolic security theorems on collision-free traces and has a functional-refinement proof.
results.detail: The symbolic result assumes two provisioned parties with pinned identities, fresh coins, bounded inputs, modeled AArch64 Linux execution and conforming hooks. Attacker knowledge comes from public setup values, bundles, wire messages and allowed leaks or inversions. Side channels are outside scope. At a collision, the guarantee covers the preceding prefix.
results.quote: We prove that the machine code computes exactly what the model computes, and that the game run on the model is secure. A coupling argument then shows that the game run on the machine code is secure as well

results.finding: In one libsignal campaign, authors wrote 0 proof lines. The post-maintenance manual edit rate was unmeasured.
results.detail: The reported absence of human proof authorship applies to this campaign. The paper reports that early source changes or recompilation required large proof repairs and gives no manual-edit percentage for those repairs.

results.finding: For one libsignal verification campaign, the five-person team reported four weeks of work.
results.detail: The historical comparisons involve other systems. The paper provides no baseline workflow or cost accounting for the same verification scope.
results.quote: The proof work was done by a team of five over four weeks, working in parallel on symbolic and computational proofs.

results.finding: Flit completed safety checks on 2 native SPARC benchmark binaries using their accompanying LTAL witnesses.
results.detail: The LTAL witness guides Flit in checking that a typing derivation exists. The dissertation reports that the machine-checked soundness proof connecting that derivation to the safety policy was still nearing completion.

results.finding: seL4 16.0.0 reports a completed functional correctness proof for 1 kernel configuration, MCS on 64-bit RISC-V.
results.detail: The implementation level cannot be determined from the release notes.
results.quote:
The MCS configuration for 64-bit RISC-V now has a functional correctness proof, and the functional correctness proof for
MCS on AArch64 is ongoing.

results.finding: On one system, seL4 on AArch64, Proofcraft reports completed proofs for three named security property classes.
results.detail: Three is the count of security property classes named in the announcement. The source gives no system-wide count for a Phase 3 evaluation.
results.quote:
Ryan Barry presented his
recent completion of the
seL4 security proofs on AArch64
: integrity,
confidentiality and authority confinement.

results.finding: AWS-LC (1 production library) reports running formal verification checks in CI on every change.
results.detail: The README refers readers to a separate repository for the verified API functions, caveats, and verification technology.
results.quote: the checks are run in AWS-LC’s CI on every change.

results.finding: For one PKCS#1 v1.5 parser tested in four assisted runs, the authors estimated 2.5 person-months of human effort for LLM-assisted verification.
results.detail: Prior research and methodology development counted toward the manual estimate and helped accelerate the assisted work. The assisted estimate included time spent learning to work with the LLM. All four runs required human intervention.
results.quote: We estimate the total human effort for this work to be approximately 2.5 person-months, compared to 6 person-months required for the manual proof.

results.finding: Across 14 evolved OCaml programs, completing Sisyphus-assisted Coq proof repairs took under 20 minutes of manual work per program.
results.detail: One author timed manual specification and proof of the original versions. Another timed completion of residual obligations after Sisyphus ran. The study did not time manual verification of the same updated versions.
results.quote:
As can be seen from the table, all obligations took fewer than 20 minutes to dispatch, while
specifying and proving the original programs took considerably longer, demonstrating the util-
ity of Sisyphus for maintaining veriﬁed code-bases.

goal.need = "Of 912 high- or critical-severity bugs examined in stable Chrome releases, about 70% involved memory safety. Tests give little evidence about inputs they never exercise. An operator updating a network service could check, before running it, that every execution covered by the proof respects its memory and information-flow rules. At cost parity, suppliers could maintain that assurance within their ordinary development and maintenance budgets. Its value depends on the rules capturing users\u2019 needs and on the execution assumptions holding.". Reason: The kernel defect count describes one verification project, while the browser data quantify a risk to users and the revised text explains what an operator gains when software changes.

add statement by Verified Software Initiative, The Verified Software Initiative: A Manifesto, 2009: "replace unverified programs in current service and continue to evolve in a verified state.". Reason: The manifesto explicitly names continued verification as deployed software changes, a maintenance goal missing from the existing statements.

edit m1: criterion = "Before executing a supplied native-code binary, the consumer checks its accompanying proof against the binary and the consumer\u2019s published safety policy. Validation must establish that the code obeys the policy whenever the stated entry conditions hold."; refs = [5, 14]. Reason: The four packet filters and their particular access rules are evidence from one experiment; the reusable test is validation of the supplied proof against the consumer’s policy.

edit m2: criterion = "A proof assistant checks that every observable behaviour of the implementation under the stated execution assumptions is permitted by its abstract functional specification. Identify the implementation level to which the theorem applies.". Reason: The revised criterion states what refinement requires across implementations and leaves the ARM kernel’s coverage and exclusions with its result.

edit m3: criterion = "Machine-check a theorem covering every successful compilation in the supported source language. When the source program has defined behaviour, every observable behaviour of the generated assembly must be permitted by the source semantics.". Reason: The compiler version and supported architectures belong with the result, while the test concerns what the compiler theorem guarantees for successful compilations.

edit m4: criterion = "Prove that the executable refines the source semantics used in the functional-correctness proof. For that same executable and configuration, establish that the functional specification and the information-flow policy both hold. State the execution assumptions and the observations covered by the information-flow theorem.". Reason: The existing criterion describes one compiler run and leaves implicit that both guarantees must apply to the same executable configuration.
